title: Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs
hook: trading communities, like Makhan Shah and Lakhi Shah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikligar Sikhs, metalworkers who once kept the Gurus' steel sharp. Your line was remember the sikligars. Whose hands did you thank? Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

Guru Nanak sometimes speaks to the listener as a trader. In one hymn he calls the listener vanjaria mitra, my merchant friend, and walks them through the night of a life watch by watch, as if it were a long trading journey. What did you set out to buy? What are you carrying home? The image would land in a world of traders: caravans of pack bullocks, boats on the rivers, goods moving from market to market. Some of those trading families became Sikhs. Two of them did something the panth still remembers.
screen: `MY MERCHANT FRIEND.` → `A LIFE AS A TRADING JOURNEY.` → `TRADERS WHO BECAME SIKHS.`

segments.voice: The Lubanas and the Vanjaras are trading communities, remembered for carrying goods across long distances by caravan and by boat. Both have Sikh families with deep roots in the panth. Sikh tradition keeps two of their names close. First, Makhan Shah Lubana. The story says his ship was caught in a storm, and he vowed an offering of gold to the Guru if he came through. He did. When he went to pay his vow, he found a crowd of men each claiming to be the Guru. So he tried a quiet test. He laid a small offering before each claimant, and each accepted it. Then he came to a man sitting apart in meditation, Tegh Bahadur, who said, in effect: you promised more than this. Makhan Shah ran up to a rooftop and shouted that he had found the Guru. Second, Lakhi Shah Vanjara. The story turns darker. After Guru Tegh Bahadur was executed in Delhi, his body lay where the authorities had left it. Tradition says Lakhi Shah, a carrier with carts and men, brought his caravan through, took the body away in the confusion, carried it home, and set his own house alight so the Guru could be cremated with honor without drawing attention. A gurdwara stands at that place today. Two traders. One found a hidden Guru; one gave up his own house for him. Guru Nanak's merchant hymn, on Ang 74, follows the trader through the watches of the night to the journey's end. In the panth's memory, these two spent their journeys on the Guru, and it still says their names.
screen: `LUBANAS AND VANJARAS: CARAVAN TRADERS.` · `MAKHAN SHAH FINDS THE HIDDEN GURU.` · `LAKHI SHAH GIVES UP HIS HOUSE.` · `ANG 74: WHAT DOES THE TRADER CARRY HOME?` · then, large: `THE TRADERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a trader. Let the breath settle first. Then call up one person whose work is buying and selling, carrying and delivering: a shopkeeper you know by face, a market vendor, a driver who brings things to your door. Think of the roads they travel and the hours they keep so that what you need is there. Breathe in, and see their face. Breathe out, and hold a plain thank-you ready for the next time you meet. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Lubana and Vanjara Sikhs. Sikhs from trading communities, among them Makhan Shah, who found the Guru, and Lakhi Shah, who gave up his house for him. Today's word.
Your line: the traders. Today, thank one person who sells you something, by name if you can, and ask how their day is going, and wait for the answer. Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Makhan Shah Lubana and Lakhi Shah Vanjara in the stories of Guru Tegh Bahadur, and Lubana and Vanjara Sikh families keep their trading heritage alongside their place in the panth.

original.note: Punjabi: a trader or merchant; Guru Nanak calls the listener vanjaria, merchant friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru's stories are only about saints and soldiers.
what it means: traders stand at two turning points in Guru Tegh Bahadur's story: his finding and his cremation.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's own hymn on Ang 74 uses the trader's language for a whole life, so the panth's traders were already in the Granth's picture.
